newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire troops join rebel army, Mobutu warned to go.
newsitem.headline: Zaire troops join rebel army, Mobutu warned to go.

text.p: Hundreds of former government soldiers lined up on Saturday to join the Zairean rebels, who gave President Mobutu Sese Seko 24 hours to leave office before they renewed their offensive.

Colonel Deward N'sau-Nzuzi took the roll-call of some 400 men of the former 21st Leopard infantry brigade, which switched to Kabila three days ago to help rebels capture Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city.
Rebel radio Voice of the People, broadcasting from the eastern town of Goma, said some of their units were just 300 km (187 miles) from the capital Kinshasa.
"Mr Mobutu has just 24 hours thanks to the extreme generosity of the Alliance. He has only two choices -- to resign or to go into exile," the radio said.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila had declared from Thursday a three-day "pause" in the advance of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire (AFDL) after the capture of Lubumbashi to put pressure on Mobutu, Zaire's ruler since 1965 but now ailing with cancer.

"As you can see, we've discarded the FAZ (Forces Armees de Zaire) uniforms and the men are in civvies until we get the new uniforms of the Alliance," Colonel N'sau told Reuters in the newly captured capital of Shaba province.
"I'm registering all the men of my former brigade who are ready to continue fighting for Kabila and seeking out the best elements. Some will be demobbed," he added.
In the arms magazine, men were busy emptying the Leopard brigade's ageing arsenal. Heavy and light machineguns, combat rifles, rocket launchers and boxes of bullets were stacked neatly on the floor.

"This stuff is all pretty old, from around 1975," said a lieutenant. But he quickly assembled a lethal-looking Korean rocket launcher, using a round that came straight out of its original plastic packing.

Colonel N'sau said he never had any doubt about switching from Mobutu's army. "My men were neither paid nor fed. Their uniforms were seven years old. It is time for a change here after 30-odd years of Mobutu."
With Lubumubashi nearly back to normal and bearing virtually no war damage, the prospect of genuine change was beginning to preoccupy some citizens wary of opportunist politicians.

"New revolution, new men," said Jean-Luc Kahamba Mukengo of the opposition National Federalist Party (PNF). "We don't want people who've been living off the Mobutu system worming their way into the new government."

Longtime Mobutu opponents in the city were angered on Friday to see the governor of Shaba province, Kyungu wa Kumwanza, driving in his official limousine with a white rebel flag, cheered as if he were the "liberator" of the city.

At the Mokador in the centre of town, serving cafe-au-lait and croissants, head waiter Kaiser Nzengu said: "Who does he think he is anyway? He was in that position courtesy of Mobutu. The quicker Kabila gets here and organizes elections the better."

For Colonel Kinene Nsimba, 54, of Mobutu's elite Division Speciale Presidentielle, or presidentual guard, the war was over. Sent to add backbone to Lubumbashi's defences, he said he had strayed into a rebel-held position and been captured.
On Saturday, he emerged barefoot from a dank basement cell in dirty civilian clothing to be photographed, with rebel AK-47s pointed at his chest.
